headline: High: shared local filesystem, broad shell/network, and auto-execute options make Cursor↔Windsurf prone to prompt injection, data leakage, and destructive cross-agent actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor and Windsurf both use clipboard/files and MCP, and Cursor explicitly shares state via the local filesystem. That creates a default bridge where one agent can ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. The pathway is plausible without unusual setup, but the main blast radius is instruction hijacking rather than immediate irreversible harm.
conditions: IF either agent reads files written by the other as instructions or prompts, injection is possible.
IF the shared local filesystem is used as an exchange channel, attacker-controlled content can cross agents.
mitigations: Disable shared workspace handoff between the two editors.
Keep one agent on a separate project directory.
Avoid copy-pasting agent output into the other agent.
Review any file the other agent wrote before opening it as prompt material.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging or sandboxed handoff storage.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code and open files, and both can read the filesystem with broad network egress. Cursor also handles clipboard contents and model-provider API keys, while Windsurf uses a model proxy. In a shared workspace, sensitive file contents can flow into either backend by default, so leakage is plausible in normal use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace, file contents can be exposed to both backends.
IF secrets are stored in open files or clipboard, either agent may ingest them.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate repos or clones for each agent.
Clear clipboard before switching agents.
Restrict network access for one agent during sensitive edits.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, git modification, and broad network egress, while Cursor explicitly shares state via the local filesystem. That is a direct write-write conflict on the same mutable resources, and concurrent edits or git operations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The default overlap is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF both agents modify git state without coordination, repository corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid simultaneous git operations.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestrator-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents are autonomous coding agents with shell and git authority, so one agent’s output can become the other’s action plan. Cursor’s multi-step agent loop and Windsurf’s Cascade loop can amplify a mistaken assumption into edits, commands, or commits without independent verification. That makes downstream errors likely and potentially destructive.
conditions: IF one agent’s generated plan is copied into the other without review, errors can cascade.
IF either agent is allowed to execute commands automatically, mistaken outputs can become actions.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Disable auto-run or auto-execute modes.
Have the second agent verify diffs before acting.
Limit each agent to read-only analysis on critical tasks.
requires-engineering: add structured verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are closed-source and docs-only, but the visible compliance surface is mostly similar: local editor processes, workspace files, and optional BYOK secrets. I do not see a documented residency or certification mismatch in the profiles, so only a small compliance gap is evident from the available evidence.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in either workspace, vendor policy differences may matter.
IF one deployment requires stricter retention or residency guarantees than the other, a mismatch can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools.
Review vendor privacy and retention settings.
Use separate accounts for sensitive work.
Disable optional telemetry where available.
requires-engineering: obtain formal compliance attestations before use.
